name: Conditioning Solution Preparation
description: Prepares an optimal cut-flower conditioning solution to facilitate rapid water uptake and deliver essential carbohydrates without inducing osmotic shock or bacterial blooms. The optimal formulation requires 800 ml of water heated to 41 °C combined with 8 g of flower food powder, establishing an exact concentration of 10 g/L.

learned_parameters.label: Water Volume
learned_parameters.rationale: Volume pairs with powder to dictate ionic concentration. Keeping 8 g powder but reducing water to 500 ml (attempt #6) concentrated the solution excessively (sub-score 6/100, score 43.4). Increasing volume to 1050 ml (attempt #8) diluted it (sub-score 64/100, score 78.1). The baseline 800 ml (attempt #5, score 100.0) provides the exact volume for 8 g of powder to yield the required 10 g/L concentration. Measured: Total score by value: 500 ml -> 43.4, 800 ml -> 8.1, 800 ml -> 40.0, 800 ml -> 40.7, 800 ml -> 41.5, 800 ml -> 48.1, 800 ml -> 100.0, 1050 ml -> 78.1.

learned_parameters.label: Flower Food Powder
learned_parameters.rationale: The powder provides biocides and carbohydrates. At 4 g in 800 ml (attempts #1–#3), the concentration sub-score was only 14/100 due to under-dosing. Dosing 12 g (attempt #4) or 16 g (attempt #7) caused chemical burns with sub-scores of 14 and 0 respectively. Exactly 8 g (attempt #5, score 100.0) yields the ideal 100/100 concentration sub-score. Measured: Total score by value: 2 g -> 40.7, 4 g -> 8.1, 4 g -> 41.5, 4 g -> 48.1, 8 g -> 43.4, 8 g -> 78.1, 8 g -> 100.0, 12 g -> 48.1, 16 g -> 40.0.

learned_parameters.label: Water Temperature
learned_parameters.rationale: Water temperature directly governs stem uptake rate and embolism clearance. At 16 °C (attempt #1), Water Temperature sub-score was 0/100 (total score 8.1). Increasing to 35 °C (attempt #2) raised the sub-score to 84/100 (total score 41.5). Reaching 41 °C (attempts #3, #5, #10) achieved a perfect 100/100 sub-score, confirming the standard warm conditioning practice supported by cut flower handling research. Measured: Best sub-score 100/100 at 41 °C. Tried 16 °C (sub-score 0) to 41 °C (sub-score 100). Sub-score stayed at or above 80 between 35 °C and 41 °C.

control_effects.effect: Dilutes or concentrates the powder ratio. With 8 g powder, lowering volume to 500 ml dropped concentration sub-score to 6 (#6), whereas increasing volume to 1050 ml dropped concentration sub-score to 64 (#8). A volume of 800 ml delivers the optimal 100 sub-score (#5). Measured: Total score by value: 500 ml -> 43.4, 800 ml -> 8.1, 800 ml -> 40.0, 800 ml -> 40.7, 800 ml -> 41.5, 800 ml -> 48.1, 800 ml -> 100.0, 1050 ml -> 78.1.

Controls carbohydrate availability and biocide levels. Low powder values (2 g scored 40.7 in #9, 4 g scored 48.1 in #3) caused dilution and blossom starvation. Excessive powder (12 g scored 48.1 in #4, 16 g scored 40.0 in #7) caused chemical burn. Exactly 8 g in 800 ml maximized concentration to 100/100 in #5 and #10. Measured: Total score by value: 2 g -> 40.7, 4 g -> 8.1, 4 g -> 41.5, 4 g -> 48.1, 8 g -> 43.4, 8 g -> 78.1, 8 g -> 100.0, 12 g -> 48.1, 16 g -> 40.0.

Controls water uptake viscosity and vascular clearing. Shifting from 16 °C to 35 °C improved the temperature sub-score from 0 to 84 (#1 to #2), and reaching 41 °C achieved a flawless 100 sub-score across attempts #3 through #10. Measured: Best sub-score 100/100 at 41 °C. Tried 16 °C (sub-score 0) to 41 °C (sub-score 100). Sub-score stayed at or above 80 between 35 °C and 41 °C.
4 g / 800 ml (5 g/L) scores 14/100 and is flagged as too dilute (#1-#3). Measured: Relation 'Preservative Concentration' depends on several controls together; best sub-score 100/100.

steps: Measure 800 ml of clean tap or filtered water into the conditioning vessel.
Heat or adjust the water temperature to exactly 41 °C to minimize water viscosity and prevent air embolisms in cut stems.
Weigh out 8 g of commercial flower food powder.
Add the 8 g of flower food powder to the 800 ml of 41 °C water to reach the target 10 g/L preservative concentration.
Stir thoroughly until all powder is completely dissolved before inserting flower stems.
caveats: Preservative concentration is an interactive ratio of food powder mass to water volume; altering water volume without adjusting powder proportionally degrades the concentration sub-score.
Cold water below 35 °C dramatically hinders hydration rate through cut stem vessels and traps embolisms.
Overdosing powder above 10 g/L creates hypertonic solution conditions that scorch petal edges via reverse osmosis.
'Preservative Concentration' depends on several controls together, not one alone.

problems.problem: The nutrient solution is too dilute; bacteria thrive while the opening blossoms starve of carbohydrates.
problems.fix: Increase flower food powder or decrease excess water volume to restore the ratio to 8 g per 800 ml (10 g/L).

problems.problem: The water is too cold; viscous water and trapped air embolisms delay stem rehydration.
problems.fix: Raise the water temperature from cool levels (e.g., 16 °C) up to the warm conditioning optimum of 41 °C.
